proposals.relationship: Cronon presents Crosby’s studies of migrating organisms and introduced pathogens as practical lessons of environmental history.
proposals.evidence_note: Cronon’s own 1993 presidential address, pp. 8 and 10, explicitly footnotes these lessons to The Columbian Exchange (1972) and Ecological Imperialism (1986). This is a specified use in explaining the field’s practical value, not evidence that every part of Cronon’s method comes from Crosby. Cronon also insists on particular places and times and on the limits of general environmental lessons. Both cited Crosby books remain unread in full. Note 16 is on printed p. 21; note 25 is on p. 22. This fresh check corrects the inherited collective locator placing both notes on p. 22 without replacing the old source record.
primary_locators: The Uses of Environmental History (1993), p. 8 migration-and-organisms bullet with n. 16, p. 10 first bullet with n. 25; notes 16 and 25 on pp. 21 and 22 respectively.

proposals.relationship: Worster uses Crosby’s ecological-imperialism concept in the Kentucky bluegrass example; Crosby separately endorses Worster’s agroecological research agenda.
proposals.evidence_note: Two distinct intellectual actions in the same 1990 round table are retained in one directed contribution record. Fresh selected English primary transcription of Worster’s 1990 essay, pp. 1087–1089, particularly p. 1088 and n. 4. Worster names the concept and its source, while warning that the bluegrass example is more complicated than simple environmental determinism. This is a specific conceptual resource in his argument, not a claim that Crosby originated all of Worster’s environmental history. The English page images were not available; the witness is a page-labelled transcription. The original source’s earlier Portuguese-translation and 1993-reprint reading scopes remain distinct. Crosby’s own response to Transformations of the Earth, first page (1107), says that the essay continues their agreement and argues that agroecosystems deserve greater historical attention. He contrasts agriculture’s long history with the industrial revolution and discusses soil, water and simplified biota. This is a documented response and endorsement, distinct from Worster’s use of Crosby’s ecological-imperialism concept. Only the publisher’s first-page facsimile was read; pp. 1108–1110 and Worster’s later reply remain unread. No claim of complete agreement across those unread pages or the entire round table is made.
primary_locators: Transformations of the Earth (1990), printed p. 1088, paragraph beginning Actually, the facts in the case are more complicated, and n. 4 citing Crosby’s Ecological Imperialism (1986).
An Enthusiastic Second (1990), printed p. 1107, opening paragraph and subsequent agriculture/soil/water discussion; publisher first-page preview.

proposals.relationship: In his 2004 preface Crosby identifies Pomeranz’s Great Divergence as the clearest exposition of the new scenario linking European industrialization to overseas ecological resources.
proposals.evidence_note: Crosby’s own second-edition preface, pp. xv–xx, explicitly names Pomeranz at p. xvii, n. 1, then develops the scenario through overseas ecosystems, resources and labour, and says that he is proud to have contributed to it. This later self-positioning is dated 2004 and is not projected into the original 1986 book. The direction records Pomeranz as an acknowledged resource for this later framing, not priority for Crosby’s original ecological-imperialism argument or proof that Pomeranz supplied every assertion in the preface. Pomeranz’s whole book and Crosby’s chapters 2–12 remain unread.
primary_locators: Ecological Imperialism, second edition (2004), Preface to the new edition, pp. xv–xx; specifically xvii, n. 1, and continuation xviii–xx.
